issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette:
Rohan is a 37-year-old South Asian man who works as a licensed psychologist in private practice. He is married and, until recently, considered himself professionally resilient - someone who had spent his career helping others process trauma while remaining, he believed, largely untouched by it. That self-understanding collapsed eighteen months ago when he was present at a public venue during a terrorist attack. He had been attending a conference in a downtown hotel when gunmen opened fire in the lobby. Rohan was on the mezzanine level, separated from the exits, pressed against a wall in the dark after the lights failed, listening to the shots echo through the marble atrium below. He could not move, could not call for help without risking detection, and could not know whether the men with weapons were ascending the stairwell toward him. For nearly forty minutes he lay still in the dark, entirely without agency, certain he was going to die. It was the complete absence of control - not the violence itself, but his utter inability to act - that seemed to lodge most deeply in him.

In the weeks that followed, Rohan found that ordinary moments could collapse without warning back into that mezzanine. Gunshot sounds - a car backfiring, a door slamming sharply in the corridor outside his office - would strip the present away entirely. Waking in the dark became its own ordeal; the disorientation of those first seconds before full consciousness returned him, reliably, to the hotel floor. Situations in which he felt he lacked control - a delayed train, a full waiting room, a conversation he could not redirect - carried an urgency that felt physiologically indistinguishable from danger. These triggers arrived not as memories he could examine but as experiences that reinstated the original helplessness, and in doing so they confirmed what he had quietly come to believe: that the world was genuinely dangerous and that he was powerless within it. The feeling was not abstract. It was the specific, bodily certainty of a man who had lain in the dark waiting to be shot.

To manage the unbearable quality of these states, Rohan began making adjustments. He stopped scheduling evening clients, telling himself it was a boundary issue, though the truth was that driving home in the dark had become something he needed to avoid. He began drinking - wine with dinner that became wine before dinner, and then a second glass kept close during late paperwork. He started taking a prescribed sleep aid nightly, well beyond the recommended duration. In sessions, when material became emotionally dense, he noticed himself drifting - not dissociating in any clinical sense he would have named, but retreating to a kind of internal neutrality, a world of his own that asked nothing of him. These strategies quieted the acute distress, but they also narrowed his life in ways that fed back into the very triggers he was trying to suppress. Avoiding stressors meant he was never in situations where he could discover that loss of control was survivable. The alcohol and medication blunted the evenings but made his mornings foggier, and the grogginess of waking - disoriented, slow - made the dark more threatening, not less. The drift into fantasy during sessions meant he was less present, less effective, and when clients failed to improve, the sense that he could not prevent bad outcomes intensified.

What frightened Rohan most was what he saw when he looked at himself honestly. He had become unrecognisable. The man who had trained in trauma-focused therapy, who had sat with survivors and understood, intellectually, every mechanism now operating inside him - that man felt entirely absent. In his place was someone who drank to sleep, who flinched at car doors, who could not sit in a dark room. The gap between who he had been and who he was now was its own source of distress, deepening his conviction that something irreversible had happened to him, that the world had shown him its true nature and he could not unsee it.

He sought help after his wife told him, quietly and without accusation, that she no longer recognised him either. He arrived at his first appointment hoping to recover the person he used to be, and terrified that he had already waited too long.
